cases.n: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.place: Guatemala City (Secretaría de la Paz; Hogar Elisa Martínez)
cases.victims_note: 333 adoption files reviewed, a sample of 670 adoptions recorded for 1977–1989; UPI/CNN reported the commission found at least 333 children taken and sold; the national search commission estimates about 5,000 children disappeared
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.cover: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received
cases.d: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cite: Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, Secretaría de la Paz, 'Las adopciones y los derechos humanos de la niñez guatemalteca, 1977-1989', September 2009; UPI, 12 Sept 2009

cases.n: Bolivia — two former Jesuit provincials convicted for not reporting Fr Alfonso Pedrajas (2025)
cases.victims_note: 'at least 85 minors' per Pedrajas's own diary (1972–2000), many of them Indigenous scholarship students at a boarding school; 18 victims' complaints were presented at trial
cases.cover: The court found the provincials knew of allegations against Pedrajas and did not report them to police; prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba in May 2023
cases.d: On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, Jesuit provincials of Bolivia in 1993–1999 and 1999–2007, to one year in prison each, plus costs, compensation to victims and psychological treatment, for knowing of allegations against Fr Alfonso Pedrajas and not reporting them. Pedrajas, who died in 2009, wrote in a diary published by El País in 2023 that he abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000. Prosecutors presented 18 victims' complaints and 34 witnesses and said they would pursue other priests named at trial. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia.
cases.cite: Bolivian court judgment, 2 Sept 2025, as reported by Reuters (via BishopAccountability.org)

cases.n: Paraguay — Truth and Justice Commission: sexual slavery of girls by senior officers of the Stroessner regime
cases.who: Senior military and police officers of the Stroessner regime; procurers who took girls from their families
cases.d: Paraguay's Comisión de Verdad y Justicia, created by law in October 2003, presented its final report on 28 August 2008 after collecting more than 2,000 testimonies on the 1954–1989 dictatorship. Its conclusions state that sexual violence against women and girls was encouraged by the repressive apparatus and reached its extreme in 'sexual slavery of girls practised by senior officers of the regime', and that young children were exploited economically and sexually in military posts at the service of officers. The commission heard reports of girls as young as seven being taken from their homes for officers and recorded that 10.8% of victims were minors at the time; it warned of large under-reporting of sexual violence.
cases.cite: Comisión de Verdad y Justicia del Paraguay, Informe Final, Conclusiones y Recomendaciones, Asunción, 28 Aug 2008; Amnesty International, 13 Aug 2008

cases.n: Yemen — UN Group of Eminent Experts: rape of boys and girls by armed forces; sexual violence against recruited girls
cases.place: Aden (Security Belt Forces facilities); also Ta'izz, Sana'a, Ibb
cases.who: Security Belt Forces; Yemeni 35th Armoured Brigade; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa; Houthi de facto authorities
cases.d: The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 (A/HRC/42/17) that Security Belt Forces raped 18 women, four boys and a girl in 2016–2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden; members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy; and Houthi detention sites saw sexual violence against a 17-year-old boy. Its September 2020 report found credible accounts that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13–17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.
cases.cite: Report of the Group of Eminent International and Regional Experts on Yemen, A/HRC/42/17 (Aug 2019) and A/HRC/45/6 (Sept 2020); Al Jazeera, 9 Sept 2020

cases.n: Nepal — National Human Rights Commission national reports on trafficking: an estimated 5,000 children trafficked in a year
cases.victims_note: NHRC estimate of children among about 35,000 Nepalis trafficked in the year before its 2019 report; 374 trafficked children rescued inside Nepal
cases.who: Trafficking networks moving women and girls across the open border to India and on to third countries
cases.d: Nepal's National Human Rights Commission publishes national reports on trafficking in persons, especially women and children (from 2012–13). Its report released in August 2019 estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in the previous year, including 5,000 children, and that 1.5 million were at risk. It said nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year, where they are taken for the sex trade, forced labour or domestic work or moved to third countries, and that the open border makes this hard to control.
cases.cite: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, national report on trafficking in persons (2019); The Kathmandu Post, 6 Aug 2019

cases.n: Nepal — Hague Conference mission finds regular falsification of papers to make children 'adoptable' (2010)
cases.who: Child-care homes and intermediaries in Nepal's intercountry adoption system; foreign adoption agencies
cases.d: At the request of Nepal's Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare, the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law sent a technical assistance mission to Nepal on 23–27 November 2009; its report is dated 4 February 2010. It cited evidence that documents were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin, age and status, and that this continued under the 2008 rules. It said the USD 5,000 per-child payment and USD 10,000 annual agency fee created strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care, and that Nepal had no data on adoptable children.
cases.cite: Hague Conference on Private International Law, Permanent Bureau, 'Report of Technical Assistance Mission to Nepal, 23-27 November 2009', 4 Feb 2010

cases.n: Turkey — parliamentary research commission on child abuse after the Ensar Foundation dormitory case (2016)
cases.place: Ankara (Grand National Assembly); triggered by Karaman
cases.who: Dormitories run by the Ensar Foundation and KAİMDER in Karaman; student dormitories nationally
cases.d: On 24 March 2016 the Turkish Grand National Assembly unanimously set up a research commission on preventing child abuse after sexual abuse of boys at dormitories run by the Ensar Foundation and KAİMDER in Karaman. It began work in April, visited only Karaman, and its draft report in October 2016 recommended that the Education Ministry license and inspect student dormitories, a permanent children's rights committee, a child-protection coordination centre, criminal-record checks for child-facing jobs and wider penal definitions of abuse. Opposition (CHP) members filed a dissent saying the report relied on general data, did not visit state institutions, prisons or camps, and did not name responsible administrators; a provincial report given to the commission blamed the victims' families.
cases.cite: TBMM Çocuk İstismarını Önleme Araştırma Komisyonu report (2016); Diken, 8 July 2016; BirGün, 15 June and 13 Oct 2016; bianet, 2 Nov 2016

cases.n: Zimbabwe — Gender Commission inquiry into sexual exploitation of girls and child marriage in apostolic sects (2021–2023)
cases.place: Harare (Zimbabwe Gender Commission); sect sites in Marange and Marondera
cases.victims_note: over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation received and investigated by the Commission in 2022 (all settings, not only sects)
cases.who: Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect and other apostolic church branches
cases.d: After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect shrine in 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened an investigation under its Act on 24 September 2021 into institutionalised sexual exploitation and abuse of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects. Its preliminary findings reported compulsory virginity testing, pledging and forced marriage in the Marange sect, and an earlier 2020 probe of Marondera branches found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as 'wives-in-waiting' and given to older men. Its 2022 report said it had investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation and called for legislation regulating faith-based organisations.
cases.cite: Zimbabwe Gender Commission, General Notice 2733 of 2021; The Herald (Zimbabwe), 2021; ZGC 2022 report as reported by CITE, 15 June 2023

In these the map's records are UN CAAC verifications, US TIP reports, press or NGO reports.

Leads not added: (1) UN Special Rapporteur on the sale and sexual exploitation of children, country visit report on the Dominican Republic (A/HRC/37/60/Add.1, 2018), seen only as a search result. I treated Special Rapporteur country visits as outside 'commission of inquiry / fact-finding mission'; if the map decides to count them, many countries in this list would gain an item. (2) Senegal talibé mapping (above). (3) Peru: the Manta y Vilca judgment (2024) on rapes of women and girls at army bases in Huancavelica is a single trial, not added. (4) International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur (2005) and UN COI on Burundi: sexual violence findings not specific to children; not checked in detail.

Borderline calls: Bolivia 2025 judgment is a cover-up conviction about one abuser, kept because it is the only court finding on the Jesuit province's handling; the existing record bol-pedrajas-jesuits (status 'reported') could instead be upgraded and this record merged into it. Turkey 2016 commission covers child abuse in general; kept because it was set up after the Ensar dormitory case and its recommendations target dormitories. Zimbabwe ZGC: a standalone final report was not found; findings come from the Herald (2021) and the Commission's 2022 report as reported by CITE. Yemen: individual figures from two reports are listed in d; no total victim count is given because the Group gives none. Nepal NHRC figures are estimates.

Placement: Yemen at Aden (most child-specific findings there); Nepal NHRC at its Lalitpur seat; Turkey at the parliament in Ankara; Zimbabwe at Harare; Bolivia at Cochabamba (the court was not named; the sentence is to be served at San Sebastián prison, Cochabamba).
